C4.1.q: What is an LFO used for?
options: Playing a very low bass note you can hear
Moving a control up and down, over and over
Shaping a control once per note, then stopping
Making a held note play in tune
C4.1.why: An LFO is an oscillator too slow to hear, so you send it to a control and it keeps moving that control.

C4.1.q: You want the level to jump between two positions instead of gliding. What do you change?
options: The rate, to a faster setting
The shape, to Sine
The rate, to a slower setting
The shape, to Square
C4.1.why: Shape is the path the LFO takes, and a square jumps between two positions.

C4.1.q: What happens when the rate is turned all the way up?
options: The movement blurs into a buzz that is part of the tone
The note swells slowly enough to count each rise
The LFO stops moving the control at all
The note chops cleanly on and off, twice a second
C4.1.why: Very fast movement stops sounding like movement and becomes part of the tone.

C4.1.q: LFO 1 is sent to Osc A level. You slow the Rate to about half a cycle a second. What do you hear?
options: A slow swell you can count, up then down
A quick flutter in the level
A lower pitch on the same note
A steady note with no movement
C4.1.why: Rate is how often the LFO repeats, so a slow rate gives a slow swell you can count.

C4.1.q: You hold a note while LFO 1 is not connected to anything. What do you hear?
options: A note swelling and fading
A low buzz from the LFO itself
A steady note
A note that flutters quickly
C4.1.why: You do not listen to an LFO itself, so until it is sent to a control the note stays steady.

C4.2.q: What does sending an LFO to the cutoff do?
options: It makes the note waver sharp and flat
It switches the filter off between notes
It opens and closes the filter by itself
It holds the filter open at one steady brightness
C4.2.why: An LFO on the cutoff turns it up and down for you, so the filter opens and closes by itself.

C4.2.q: The wobble is too shallow: the cutoff barely swings. Which setting do you raise?
options: Rate
Shape
Resonance
Amount
C4.2.why: Amount is how far the cutoff swings, so raising it gives a deeper wobble.

C4.2.q: While the filter wobbles, you turn the Cutoff knob up. What changes?
options: The wobble gets faster
The whole wobble moves brighter
The wobble swings further
The wobble stops moving
C4.2.why: The cutoff knob sets the middle of the swing, so turning it shifts the whole wobble brighter or darker.

C4.2.q: You change the wobble's Shape to Saw. What does each wub do now?
options: Sweeps upward, then snaps shut
Flips between two filter positions
Glides smoothly open and closed
Stays open, then fades to silence
C4.2.why: A saw ramps and drops, so each wub is a rising sweep followed by a snap shut.

C4.2.q: You want each sweep of the filter to have a vowel-like "wow". What does the filter need?
options: A faster rate
A square shape
A higher cutoff
Some resonance
C4.2.why: With some resonance on the filter, each sweep of the cutoff has a vowel-like wow to it.

C4.3.q: An LFO makes a note waver sharp and flat. Where is it sent, and what is that called?
options: To pitch: vibrato
To level: tremolo
To level: vibrato
To pitch: tremolo
C4.3.why: An LFO on pitch is vibrato, and an LFO on level is tremolo.

C4.3.q: Why does vibrato need a much smaller amount than tremolo?
options: Level is far more sensitive than pitch
An LFO on pitch always runs faster
Pitch is far more sensitive than level
A small amount makes the LFO slower
C4.3.why: Pitch is far more sensitive than level, so a tiny amount is enough and more becomes a siren.

C4.3.q: Can one note have vibrato and tremolo together?
options: No, only one LFO can run at a time
Yes, but only at exactly the same speed
No, pitch movement cancels level movement
Yes, with two LFOs, each on its own control
C4.3.why: Several LFOs can run at once, each on its own control and at its own speed.

C4.3.q: Your vibrato has turned into a siren. How do you get a gentle waver back?
options: Bring the Amount right down to a tiny value
Raise the Amount to a large value
Send the LFO to Osc A level instead
Switch on a second LFO
C4.3.why: On pitch a tiny amount gives a gentle waver, and a larger one sweeps across several notes like a siren.

C4.3.q: Two LFOs are moving two knobs at once. How can you see which LFO moves which knob?
options: Each knob shows its LFO's name as a label
Each knob wears a ring in its LFO's colour
The knobs turn at two different speeds
The LFO panels sit beside their knobs
C4.3.why: A knob moved by an LFO wears a ring in that LFO's colour, cyan for LFO 1 and green for LFO 2.

C4.4.q: Why set an LFO's speed in beats instead of cycles per second?
options: So its movement swings further
So its movement lands on the beat
So it restarts with every key press
So it runs too fast to hear
C4.4.why: A speed set in beats ties the LFO to the tempo, so it stops drifting against the beat.

C4.4.q: An LFO repeats every 1 beat. You turn the tempo down. What happens to the wobble?
options: It keeps its speed and drifts off the click
It stops until you play a new note
It slows down together with the click
It changes to two wobbles per click
C4.4.why: A synced LFO follows the tempo and stays in the same place in the bar.

C4.4.q: Which setting gives three wobbles per click, the rolling triplet feel?
options: Half a beat
4 beats
1 beat
A third of a beat
C4.4.why: A third of a beat fits three wobbles into each beat, which is a triplet.

C4.4.q: You set "Repeats every" to 4 beats. What do you hear?
options: One slow sweep per bar
Four wobbles per click
Two wobbles per click
One wobble per click
C4.4.why: Repeating every 4 beats, the LFO makes one slow sweep for each bar.

C4.4.q: This LFO is set to run free. You press a key a little late. What does the wobble do?
options: It starts late and stays behind the click
It drifts slowly against the click
It still keeps time with the click
It waits for the next bar to begin
C4.4.why: Running free here means the LFO keeps time with the click however late or early you press a key.

C4.5.q: An LFO is set to Free. You strike the same key several times. What do you hear?
options: Each note begins somewhere different in the movement
Every note begins in exactly the same way
Each note starts steady and the movement grows
Only the first note has any movement
C4.5.why: A Free LFO runs on regardless of your playing, so each note catches it wherever it happens to be.

C4.5.q: Which setting suits a rhythmic bass, where every note should move the same way?
options: Free
Rise
Restart
A faster rate
C4.5.why: Restart begins the shape again with every note, so it is consistent and predictable.

C4.5.q: With a Rise of about one second, how do short and long notes differ?
options: Long notes stay plain; short notes get the movement
Short notes stay plain; long notes get the movement
Both get full movement from the first instant
Short notes move faster than long notes
C4.5.why: Rise fades the movement in, so long notes get more of it than short ones.

C4.5.q: A vibrato LFO is set to Restart, with no Rise. When does the vibrato begin on each note?
options: After the note is held a while
Only on the longest notes
At a different moment each time
From the first instant of the note
C4.5.why: With Restart and no fade-in, the vibrato is on from the first instant of every note.

C4.5.q: Every note of your pad moves in exactly the same way and sounds mechanical. What do you change?
options: Switch Start to Free
Switch Start to Restart
Turn the Rise up
Send the LFO to pitch
C4.5.why: Free lets the LFO run on, so each note catches it somewhere different and the pad sounds varied.

C4.6.q: What is a drawn LFO shape?
options: One smooth curve that plays once per note
The four basic shapes played one after another
A sine with its rate turned right down
Sixteen steps, each at a height you choose
C4.6.why: A drawn shape is a row of sixteen steps that the LFO plays in order and then starts again.

C4.6.q: A drawn LFO on the filter is synced to the beat. What do its tall and short bars become?
options: Louder and quieter keys of a chord
Open and closed moments of the filter: a rhythm
Faster and slower parts of the wobble
Higher and lower notes of a melody
C4.6.why: Synced to the beat, the steps become a rhythm of bright bursts and dark gaps.

C4.6.q: Why can one held note sound like a moving bassline here?
options: The LFO plays different keys for you
Hold strikes the note again on every click
The drawn LFO moves the filter in a repeating pattern
The tempo changes the note on every beat
C4.6.why: One held note with a drawn LFO on the filter is already a pattern, made of changes in brightness.

C4.6.q: Your drawn pattern repeats every 4 beats. You set "Repeats every" to 2 beats. What do you hear?
options: The same pattern, half as fast
The same pattern, twice as fast
Only the first half of the pattern
A new pattern with fewer steps
C4.6.why: The LFO still plays the same steps in order, so a shorter repeat plays the same pattern twice as fast.

C4.6.q: You change the Shape from Sine to Drawn, before drawing anything yourself. What do you hear?
options: The same smooth sweep as the sine
Silence until you draw a bar
A staircase stepping down through the bar
Bright bursts with dark gaps between
C4.6.why: A drawn shape is a row of steps, and here it begins as a staircase stepping down through the bar.

C4.C.q: When matching a hidden moving sound, what should you decide first?
options: How fast the movement is
How far the movement goes
Whether it glides, jumps or ramps
What is moving: loudness, pitch or brightness
C4.C.why: First decide what is moving, because everything else depends on it.

C4.C.q: A hidden sound jumps between two positions instead of gliding. Which question does that answer?
options: What path the movement takes
What is being moved
How fast the movement is
How far the movement goes
C4.C.why: Gliding, jumping or ramping is the path the movement takes.

C4.C.q: What helps you judge how fast a hidden sound is moving?
options: Listening for how bright it gets
Counting it against a slow steady beat
Listening for how far it swings
Listening for whether it jumps or glides
C4.C.why: Counting the movement against a slow steady beat helps you find the rate.

C5.1.q: What are the three parts of a route?
options: A rate, a shape and an amount
An LFO, an envelope and a filter
A source, a destination and an amount
A knob, a ring and a centre
C5.1.why: A route is a source that moves, a destination knob it moves, and an amount for how far.

C5.1.q: An LFO is wobbling the cutoff. You turn the Cutoff knob down. What happens?
options: The same movement, shifted darker
The wobble gets shallower
The wobble gets slower
The route is switched off
C5.1.why: The knob sets the centre and the route adds its movement to it.

C5.1.q: Two LFOs and an envelope are all sent to the cutoff. What do you get?
options: Only the last one connected
Only the fastest of the three
No movement: they cancel out
Their movements added together
C5.1.why: Several routes on one knob add together, which builds complicated motion from simple parts.

C5.1.q: LFO 1 is sent to Filter cutoff with its Amount at exactly 0. What do you hear?
options: Nothing moving, because the route is removed
A wobble at half its depth
Silence, because the filter has closed
Nothing moving, though the route still exists
C5.1.why: A route with an amount of zero still exists, but it moves nothing.

C5.1.q: LFO 1 and LFO 3 are both sent to Filter cutoff. What does the Cutoff knob wear?
options: Two rings, one in each LFO's colour
One ring, for the faster LFO only
One ring, for the LFO sent last
No ring, because the two cancel
C5.1.why: One knob can have several routes at once, and it wears a ring for each of them.

C5.2.q: What does 'both ways' (bipolar) mean for an LFO?
options: It moves two different knobs at the same time
It swings above and below the knob's setting equally
It swings above the knob's setting and stays there
It runs forwards, then backwards, through its shape
C5.2.why: Both ways means the LFO swings above the knob's setting and below it by the same distance.

C5.2.q: Why does a one-way LFO on pitch make the whole note sound raised?
options: It swings twice as far as a both-ways LFO
It runs faster than a both-ways LFO does
It only ever goes sharp, never below the true pitch
It wavers evenly around the true pitch
C5.2.why: One way moves from the knob's setting to one side only, so the pitch only goes sharp.

C5.2.q: A square LFO on pitch is set to one way, with the amount below zero. Which trill do you hear?
options: Your note and a note below it
Your note and a note above it
A note below and a note above, never yours
No trill, because the amount is below zero
C5.2.why: With one way, the knob's own setting is always one end of the movement, so your note is always heard.

C5.2.q: A square LFO on pitch is set to Both ways. You hold a key. Which notes do you hear?
options: The held key and a note above it
Notes below and above; never the held key
The held key and a note below it
Only the held key, with no movement
C5.2.why: Both ways swings either side of the knob's setting, so the square jumps below and above and skips the held note.

C5.2.q: Envelope 2 is sent to a knob. How does it move that knob?
options: Both ways: equally above and below the knob
Both ways, but further upward than downward
One way: from the knob in one direction
Neither way until an LFO joins it
C5.2.why: An envelope is always one way: it starts from the knob and pushes in one direction.

options: How high or low the key is
How long the key is held
How hard a key is struck
How fast the note repeats
C5.3.why: Velocity is how hard a key is struck, and key position is which key it is.

C5.3.q: How does velocity behave during one note?
options: It keeps rising while the key is held
It is fixed from the moment the note starts
It swings up and down like an LFO
It falls away like an envelope
C5.3.why: Velocity and key position are each one number, decided the moment the note starts.

C5.3.q: You want harder notes to be brighter but no louder. Where do you send Velocity?
options: Note level
Key position
Nothing
Filter cutoff
C5.3.why: Velocity on the cutoff makes soft notes dull and hard notes bright, at the same loudness.

C5.3.q: Velocity is sent to nothing. You strike a key softly, then hard. What do you hear?
options: The hard note is louder
The hard note is brighter
The hard note is higher
No difference at all
C5.3.why: Until Velocity is sent to a knob, nothing is listening to how hard you play.

C5.3.q: Your bright sound gets piercing on the high keys. Which route helps?
options: Key position to Note level, amount below zero
Key position to Note level, amount above zero
Velocity to Note level, amount below zero
Key position to Filter cutoff, amount above zero
C5.3.why: Key position on Note level with an amount below zero makes high notes quieter than low ones.

C5.4.q: What does one row of the matrix show?
options: One note you played and how hard you struck it
One connection: source, what it moves, how far, which way
One knob and every other setting on its panel
One LFO with its rate, its shape and its start
C5.4.why: The matrix lists every connection, one row each, with source, destination, amount and direction.

C5.4.q: You change LFO 1's amount in its matrix row. What does the Amount knob on its panel do?
options: It stays put: the matrix overrides it
It drops to zero: only one can be used
It adds its own amount on top
It moves too: they are the same setting
C5.4.why: A row in the matrix and the control on the panel are the same setting.

C5.4.q: How do you make one LFO move the filter, the pitch and the level together?
options: Add matrix rows sending that LFO to the other knobs
Use three LFOs, all set to the same rate
Turn that LFO's amount up as far as it goes
Change the amount in its row to below zero
C5.4.why: Extra rows send one source to several knobs, so they move as one gesture.

C5.4.q: LFO 1 moves the filter and the level. You set the level row's amount to about -50. What do you hear?
options: The sound is loudest when it is brightest
The sound is quietest when it is brightest
The level stops moving altogether
The filter starts moving the other way
C5.4.why: A row with an amount below zero turns that one job upside down, so level falls as the filter opens.

C5.4.q: LFO 1 has extra rows for pitch and level. You remove the pitch row. What happens?
options: Pitch, filter and level all stop moving
Pitch is steady and the level row goes too
Pitch is steady; filter and level still move together
Nothing changes until you strike a new key
C5.4.why: Each row is one connection, so removing the pitch row leaves the filter and level rows as they were.

C5.5.q: The Cutoff knob wears two coloured dots. What does that tell you?
options: One source is moving it in both directions
One source is moving it twice as far
Two sources are moving it, one dot each
Two knobs are linked to the same source
C5.5.why: A knob wears a dot for each source that moves it, in that source's colour.

C5.5.q: What does double-clicking a dot do?
options: Removes that source's connection to the knob
Sets that source's amount to zero; the connection stays
Puts the knob itself back where it started
Sets that source's amount as high as it goes
C5.5.why: A double-click sets that source's amount to zero, and the connection is still there, doing nothing.

C5.5.q: You set LFO 1's amount with its dot on Cutoff. What does the Amount knob on the LFO 1 panel show?
options: Its old amount: the dot is separate
Zero: the dot has taken over
Both amounts added together
The same amount: it is one setting
C5.5.why: The dot, the source's Amount knob and the matrix row are the same setting.

C5.5.q: The wobble on Cutoff is too shallow. What is the quick fix, right at the knob?
options: Double-click the LFO's dot on Cutoff
Turn the Cutoff knob itself upward
Drag the ring around Cutoff wider
Drag the LFO's dot on Cutoff upward
C5.5.why: The dot is a handle: dragging it up raises that source's amount, and the ring grows as you do.

C5.5.q: You drag Envelope 2's dot on Cutoff below zero and strike a new key. How does each note behave?
options: It starts darker and opens up
It starts brighter and settles darker
It stays dark for the whole note
It wobbles more deeply than before
C5.5.why: Below zero, the envelope pushes the cutoff down from the knob and then lets go, so notes start dark and open.

C5.6.q: Besides the knobs that shape the sound, what else can a source be sent to?
options: Another source's settings, such as an LFO's rate
Nothing else: only the filter and oscillators
Only knobs that no other source is moving
Only a knob on its own panel
C5.6.why: A destination does not have to be part of the sound: a source's own settings can be destinations.

C5.6.q: A slow LFO is sent to a fast LFO's rate. What do you hear?
options: The wobble getting brighter and darker in tone
The wobble starting again with every new note
The wobble speeding up and slowing down by itself
Two steady wobbles at once on the filter
C5.6.why: A slow LFO on a fast LFO's rate makes the movement itself move.

C5.6.q: Each note's wobble should start fast and settle to its normal speed. What do you send to the LFO's rate?
options: A slow sine LFO
An envelope
A slow square LFO
Another fast LFO
C5.6.why: An envelope moves once per note, so on the rate it gives every note its own change of speed.

C5.7.q: Which knobs can a source be sent to?
options: Only the oscillator and filter knobs
Only the knobs marked Smoothest
Any knob except those on the effects
Any knob, including other sources and the effects
C5.7.why: If it is a knob, something can move it: oscillator, filter, envelopes, other sources and effects.

C5.7.q: A very fast LFO sounds grainy on one destination. Why?
options: That destination is moved only about fifty times a second
That destination is one of those marked Smoothest
That destination is moved separately for every note
That destination already has a source on it
C5.7.why: Destinations not marked Smoothest are moved about fifty times a second, which a very fast LFO outruns.

C5.7.q: An envelope is sent to Distortion drive and you play several notes. Which note does the effect follow?
options: The first note played
The lowest note played
The last note played
Each note separately
C5.7.why: Effects are shared by all notes, so a source on an effect follows the last note played.

C5.7.q: LFO 2 is moving Warp amount. You send LFO 3 to LFO 2 rate. What do you hear?
options: LFO 2's movement gets deeper and shallower
LFO 2's movement speeds up and slows down
LFO 2 stops and LFO 3 moves the warp
Both LFOs settle at the same speed
C5.7.why: A source's own knobs are knobs like any other, so LFO 3 turns LFO 2's rate up and down.

C5.7.q: Envelope 2 is sent to Distortion drive at a high amount. How does each new note sound?
options: Clean at the start, growing dirtier as it is held
Dirty for the whole note, at one fixed level
Dirty at the start, cleaning up as the envelope falls
Clean throughout, with the drive knob left alone
C5.7.why: The envelope pushes the drive up at the start of the note and lets it fall back, so each note cleans up.

C5.8.q: While you drag a source's handle, a knob lights up green. What does that mean?
options: The knob already has that source
The knob can take the source
The knob is at its highest setting
The knob is being moved by a macro
C5.8.why: A knob that can take the source lights up green as you pass over it.

C5.8.q: LFO 1 is already connected to Cutoff. You drop it on Resonance as well. What happens?
options: A matrix row is added and Cutoff stays connected
It leaves Cutoff and moves to Resonance instead
Nothing, as a source has only one connection
It takes the next free slot of a macro
C5.8.why: The first drop is the source's own connection, and later drops add matrix rows.

C5.8.q: You drop a macro on a knob. Where does the connection go?
options: Into a new row of the matrix
Over the macro's first slot
Onto the panel of LFO 1
Into the macro's next free slot
C5.8.why: A macro dropped on a knob takes its next free slot.

C5.8.q: You drag LFO 1's handle onto the Cutoff knob and let go. What do you hear?
options: Nothing until you raise the amount from zero
A wobble at once, at the full amount
Nothing until you add a matrix row
A wobble at once, at a modest amount
C5.8.why: A dropped source is connected with a modest amount, so you hear it straight away.

C5.8.q: You drop Macro 1 on the Drive knob, then turn Macro 1 up. What happens to the bass?
options: It grows dirtier as the macro rises
It grows cleaner as the macro rises
It wobbles faster as the macro rises
It stays the same until a new note
C5.8.why: The drop connected Macro 1 to Drive through its first free slot, so turning the macro up adds dirt.

C5.9.q: What does the Scaled by column do to a matrix row?
options: Sets how fast the row's own source runs
Sends the row's source to a second knob
Lets a second source set how much gets through
Adds a second source's movement on top
C5.9.why: Scaled by hands the row's amount to a second source, which decides how much of it gets through.

C5.9.q: A vibrato row is scaled by the Mod wheel, and the wheel is at the bottom. What do you hear?
options: Vibrato at the row's full amount
No vibrato at all
Vibrato at half the row's amount
Vibrato that only goes downward
C5.9.why: At the second source's lowest, nothing of the row gets through.

C5.9.q: Vibrato should grow in by itself as a note is held. What do you choose for Scaled by?
options: Velocity, playing hard notes
The Mod wheel, left at the bottom
Nothing, with a larger amount
Envelope 2, with a slow attack
C5.9.why: An envelope as the scaler brings the movement in with time, as a singer adds vibrato to a long note.

C5.9.q: A vibrato row is scaled by the Mod wheel. You bring the wheel halfway. How deep is the vibrato?
options: As deep as the row's amount
Half as deep as the row's amount
Twice as deep as the row's amount
There is no vibrato at all
C5.9.why: Between its lowest and highest, the scaling source lets a share of the row through: halfway gives half.

C5.9.q: A vibrato row is scaled by Velocity. You play soft notes, then hard ones. What do you hear?
options: Soft notes wobble; hard notes almost steady
Every note wobbles the same, hard or soft
Soft notes almost steady; hard notes wobble
Soft notes quiet and hard notes loud, none wobbling
C5.9.why: With Velocity as the scaler, how hard you play decides how much of the vibrato gets through.

C5.C.q: A hidden sound is moving. What should you find first?
options: What is moving
Which way it pushes
How far it is pushed
Whether its speed changes
C5.C.why: Find what is moving before asking how it moves.

C5.C.q: The movement sits to one side of your sound, not centred on it. What does that tell you?
options: The route is both ways
The amount is at zero
The route is one way
Two sources share the knob
C5.C.why: Movement that sits to one side of your sound is a one-way route.

C5.C.q: A hidden wobble keeps changing speed by itself. What does that suggest?
options: Its amount is below zero
A second source is on its rate
Its knob has been turned up
It is sent to two knobs
C5.C.why: Movement whose speed changes has a second source on its rate.
